| Empty tab, no prompt | Meshery Server could not reach MeshSync. Confirm the cluster shows as connected and that the broker is connected. Kanvas does not display the server's error text for terminal sessions. |
| Prompt never appears, or the shell prints an error | The container has no `/bin/sh`, is not in the Running phase, or was deleted. Errors raised while MeshSync opens the shell print in the terminal itself. |
| Session goes quiet after `exit` or a pod restart | The session ended on the cluster. Kanvas shows no closed message. Close the tab and start a new session. |

For cluster connection problems, see [Troubleshoot Kanvas]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/troubleshooting.md" >}}).

## Related

- [Stream Container Logs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/operating/log-streaming/index.md" >}}) opens in the same panel as terminal sessions.
- [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}) explains where this data comes from.
- [Resource Details]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/resource-details/index.md" >}}) lists the actions available for every resource kind.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Share a Design"
url: /kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md
description: Give specific people access to a design, set its visibility, share a link, and revoke access. Covers who can share, what a grant allows, and what fails.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Sharing opens a private design to the people you name. Each grant is for one person, and it has no access level: a person who can open the shared design can also edit it and comment on it. You can also change a design's visibility to make it open to everyone, and you can copy a link that points people to it.

This guide covers the task. For the reasoning behind the access model, read [Collaboration Model]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/collaboration/index.md" >}}). For a worked example with two people, follow [Collaborative Editing]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/collaborative-editing.md" >}}).

## Before you start

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Signed-in account | Anonymous visitors to [kanvas.new](https://kanvas.new) can design without signing in, but sharing asks them to sign in first. Layer5 Cloud also refuses a share from an anonymous session. |
| Share Design permission | Kanvas hides the Share action without it, and Layer5 Cloud checks it again when the request arrives. Layer5 Cloud checks it in the organization that owns the design's workspace. A design that is in no workspace is checked in an organization the design's owner belongs to. |
| View All Users permission | The people picker searches users through this permission. Without it the search is rejected, and the dialog does not find anyone. |
| A loaded, non-empty design | Share is unavailable while a design is empty, and while it is still loading. A new design has no link until its first save assigns it an id. |
| An unpublished design | Share is hidden for a published design. |
| A remote provider | Under the local provider, sharing returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented. See [Feature Availability by Plan]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/feature-availability.md" >}}). |

Views use the same dialog and the same grant model. Sharing a view needs the Share Views permission instead of Share Design. See [Views]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/views/index.md" >}}).

## Visibility levels

Visibility decides who can open a design without a grant.

| Visibility | Who can open it | Who can edit it |
|---|---|---|
| Private | The owner, provider administrators, and people you grant access | The same people |
| Public | Anyone with the link or the design id, including anonymous visitors | Any signed-in user |
| Published | Everyone, through the Layer5 Cloud catalog | The owner, provider administrators, and people with a grant |

A newly saved design is public, whatever visibility the client requests. Make a design private before you put sensitive architecture in it. A design cannot change visibility while it is published. See [Publish Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/publishing-designs/index.md" >}}) for the published state.

Changing visibility saves like any other edit: it raises the design's version and counts against the plan's components limit.

## Give people access

1. Open Share for the design. It is in the design's top bar, and in the menu of a design in your list of recent designs.
2. Search for the person and add them. The search covers every user on Layer5 Cloud your role may search, not only your organization. It returns ten matches at a time and nothing for an empty search.
3. Confirm the person appears in **People with Access**.

The grant takes effect immediately. The person opens the design with the link, and it also appears in their list of designs.

### What a grant allows

A grant carries no access level. It lets a person open a private design, edit and save it, comment on it, clone it, and download it. What else they can do depends on their own permissions, not on the grant: deploying, validating, and sharing each check the person's role.

| Action | Owner | Person with a grant |
|---|---|---|
| Open and edit the design | Yes | Yes |
| Comment, resolve, and reopen threads | Yes | Yes |
| Clone and download | Yes | Yes |
| Share it onward | With the Share Design permission | With the Share Design permission |
| Change visibility | Yes | Layer5 Cloud does not restrict it to the owner |
| Revoke access | Yes | With the Share Design permission |
| Delete the design | Yes, and provider administrators | No |
| Transfer ownership | Not supported | Not supported |

Most accounts hold the Share Design permission, because the default Organization Admin role includes it. Expect a collaborator to be able to share the design onward unless your organization has changed its roles. See [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}).

### Rules for grants

- The owner cannot be granted access, and the owner's access cannot be revoked.
- A person can be granted access once. A second grant for the same person is rejected.
- Grants and revokes in one request are applied independently. If one half fails, the other half stays in place, and the failure names the half: "access could not be granted" or "access could not be revoked".
- Layer5 Cloud sends an invitation email to a newly granted person only when the request asks for one. The email links to the design in the Meshery Playground.
- Each share request is recorded as an event.

### Grant access to people in another organization

A grant does not compare the person's organization with the design's. You can share a design with a user from any organization on the same Layer5 Cloud. There is no provider setting that enables or blocks this. The [cross-organization tutorial]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/stellar-saas-platform.md" >}}) walks through it.

## Share a link {#sharing-your-design-with-a-link}

Copy Link produces a link that opens the design in Kanvas. It works for private and public designs.

- **Public design:** anyone with the link can open it and, if signed in, edit it.
- **Private design:** the link only points to the design. The person also needs a grant, or an administrator role. Without one, Layer5 Cloud refuses the request, and an anonymous visitor cannot open it.

The link carries the design's id. Anyone who learns the id of a public design can open it.

## Revoke access

Remove the person from **People with Access**. The change applies at once. Their clones and any copies they made stay theirs. Comments they wrote remain in the design, because comments are part of the design.

Deleting a design removes every grant for it.

## What does not grant access

- **Teams.** The dialog finds individual users only. Layer5 Cloud accepts a grant for a team through its API, but no access check honors it, so team members gain nothing from it.
- **Workspaces.** Adding a design to a workspace, and assigning teams to that workspace, does not open a private design to those teams. Layer5 Cloud checks the owner, provider administrators, and the design's own grants. See [Workspaces]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/spaces/workspaces.md" >}}) for what a workspace does control.
- **Organization membership.** Being in the owner's organization does not open a private design.

To give a whole team access, grant each member.

## Messages and failures

| Message | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Unable to share: this design could not be loaded. Try again once it has loaded. | Share was opened while the design was still loading, or after its load failed. | Wait for the design to load, or reopen it, and open Share again. |
| Failed to load the list of people with access. | The owner or the access list could not be fetched. Kanvas shows this error instead of an empty list. | Close and reopen Share. An empty list does not mean nobody has access while this error shows. |
| Failed to update visibility. | The visibility change was rejected. | Retry. |
| Changing visibility is not supported for this kind of item. | The item has no visibility control. | Keep its current visibility. |
| A single error naming the parts that failed | A grant, a revoke, or the invitation email did not complete. Parts that succeeded stay in place. | Reopen Share, check **People with Access**, and repeat the missing part. |

After any grant or revoke, check **People with Access** before you rely on the change.

<figure>
  <img src="images/designer-share.png" alt="Share dialog showing the list of people with access, a field to add users, the private and public visibility control, and a Copy Link button" />
  <figcaption>The Share dialog: add people, review who has access, set visibility, and copy the link.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Related

- [Collaboration Model]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/collaboration/index.md" >}}) explains how access, live editing, and comments fit together.
- [Review a Design with Comments]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/reviewing-designs/index.md" >}}) covers feedback on a shared design.
- [Delete a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/deleting-a-design/index.md" >}}) explains who can delete and what disappears with a design.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Validate a Design"
url: /kanvas/guides/deploying/validating-designs/index.md
description: Check every component's configuration against its schema before you deploy, read the results, and fix what they flag.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Validation checks the configuration of each component in a design against the schema of that component's definition. It runs in your browser, needs no cluster, and changes nothing. Run it while you build to catch missing or malformed fields before a dry run or a deployment spends time on them.

## Before you start

- **Environment.** Validation runs in a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run it and shows a self-hosted-feature prompt instead.
- **A non-empty design.** The Actions menu is disabled while the design has no components. An unsaved design validates; Kanvas validates the design as it is on the canvas.
- **Permission.** On mobile, the Validate Design permission gates the action. See [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}).

## What validation checks

| Checked | Not checked |
|---|---|
| Each component's configuration against the JSON schema of its registered definition, with all errors collected per component | Relationships between components |
| Required fields, types, and formats, including 32-bit and 64-bit integers and integer-or-string values | Dependencies, namespaces, and cross-references |
| | Anything in the target cluster |

Annotation components (text, shapes, and other visual elements) carry no infrastructure and are skipped. They are counted separately in the summary.

Two cases pass silently, so a clean result does not prove every component was checked:

- A component whose definition cannot be fetched from the registry is skipped as valid.
- A design whose schema version is not a supported design version reports 0 components, 0 annotations, and no errors.

## Read the results

The results show a summary line, `<N> component(s) and <M> annotations`, and an error count. With no errors the result reads `No validation errors.`

With errors, each component that has them appears as an expandable row with its name and error count. Each error names the field by its dotted path, for example `Field "spec.ports" must have required property 'apiGroup'`. When the path is empty, the line shows the message alone. Errors are warnings: they never block you from continuing.

To fix an error, open the component and go to the field named in the path. A missing required property names the field you need to fill in.

Validation runs fresh each time you open it, so results always reflect the current design.

## Results on the canvas

Validation also marks the canvas. A component with errors shows a circular badge at its lower left holding the total number of errors, schema and dry-run errors combined. Selecting the badge expands it to two counts: a yellow triangle for schema errors and a red octagon for dry-run errors. Each opens the matching results, scrolled to that component.

Badges appear only when the **Validation Warnings** and **Deployment Errors** entries in the Layers panel are on and the render mode is Full. They are hidden in Wireframe, Medium, and View-only modes. A new validation or dry run replaces them, and loading another design clears them. Editing a component does not clear its badge, so run validation again after you fix something.

## The event it records

Validating the whole design records an informational event in the event log:

> Validation completed for '<design>' with <N> error(s) found.

The event carries the design name, the total error count, and per-component results. Validating a single component records nothing.

## Validate and dry run compared

| | Validate | Dry run |
|---|---|---|
| Checks against | Each component's schema | The Kubernetes API of each target cluster |
| Needs a cluster | No | Yes |
| Catches | Missing or malformed configuration | Everything the cluster's admission and schema checks reject |
| Speed | Immediate | One request per cluster |

Validate is the fast loop while you build. Run a [dry run]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/dry-running-a-design/index.md" >}}) before you deploy, because it is the only check that involves the cluster you are deploying to. The [deploy]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}) and [undeploy]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/undeploying-designs/index.md" >}}) flows run validation as their first step.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Visualize Pull Requests with Kanvas Snapshot"
url: /kanvas/guides/snapshots/kanvas-snapshot/index.md
description: Post a rendered snapshot of your infrastructure files as a comment on every GitHub pull request, using the Layer5 GitHub App or your own workflow.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Kanvas Snapshot posts a picture of your infrastructure as a comment on each GitHub pull request. Reviewers see which components a Kubernetes manifest, Docker Compose file, or Helm chart defines, and how they connect, before they read the YAML. The comment updates on every push to the pull request.

The snapshot runs in a GitHub Actions workflow on GitHub-hosted runners. It never touches your cluster. For how a snapshot is built and what it can and cannot do, see [Kanvas Snapshot]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/snapshots/_index.md" >}}).

You can set it up two ways. The Layer5 GitHub App path installs the workflow for you. The direct path has you add the action to a workflow you own. Both produce the same comment.

## Before you start

- A [Layer5 Cloud](https://cloud.layer5.io) account.
- A repository on github.com that holds the infrastructure file. GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab, and Bitbucket are not supported.
- Permission to install a GitHub App on the repository, and to add repository secrets and commit to the default branch.
- A plan that includes GitOps Snapshots. See [availability by plan]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/snapshots/_index.md#availability-by-plan" >}}).

## Set up with the Layer5 GitHub App

The Connect wizard for GitHub in Layer5 Cloud walks through seven stages. Running it again later updates the connection.

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| Connect | GitHub opens so you can install the Layer5 GitHub App on your user or organization and choose repositories. |
| Select repositories | Lists only repositories where the App is installed. To add one, install the App on it again. |
| Import designs | Scans the selected repositories for Helm charts, Kubernetes manifests, Docker Compose files, and Meshery designs, and imports what you pick. Import failures are counted per repository. |
| Select a design for the snapshot | You choose at most one file per repository. Cloud stores its path for that repository. At least one repository needs a selection to continue. |
| Configure secrets | Cloud generates a Layer5 Cloud API token and shows it once. You add it to each repository as a secret named `MESHERY_TOKEN`. |
| Configure workflows | Cloud commits the workflow to each selected repository. Clear the checkbox to skip this stage and install nothing. |
| Finish | Shows which repositories received the workflow. |

Cloud never writes the secret for you. Add `MESHERY_TOKEN` to each repository yourself, with that exact name, and confirm the checkbox in the wizard. The wizard generates a new token each time the secrets stage opens, and it cannot show an earlier one again. Generate tokens in Layer5 Cloud and revoke them there; see [Tokens]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/tokens.md" >}}).

### What the installed workflow does

The wizard commits `.github/workflows/kanvas.yml` to the default branch of each repository, with the commit message `Install Kanvas workflow`. If that file already exists, the wizard replaces it.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Name | Kanvas Screenshot Service |
| Triggers | `pull_request` when opened, synchronized, or reopened. Also `workflow_call`, with an optional `fileName` input that overrides the stored path. |
| Runner | `ubuntu-latest` |
| Token permissions | `actions: read`, `contents: write`, `security-events: write`, `statuses: write`, `pull-requests: write`, `id-token: write` |
| Authentication | `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` to comment, `secrets.MESHERY_TOKEN` for Layer5 Cloud |
| Input file | The path you selected for that repository |
| Input type | `Kubernetes Manifest`, always |

Two behaviors matter after install:

- **The input type is always `Kubernetes Manifest`.** If the file you chose is a Docker Compose file or a Helm chart, edit `application_type` in the committed workflow to `Docker Compose` or `Helm Chart`.
- **The workflow is built from the latest template at install time.** Installing the same repository twice on different days can produce a different workflow. Review the committed file before you rely on it.

Per-repository install results are:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Workflow added` with a commit link | The file was committed. |
| `Workflow already exists, try deleting it first at ./.github/workflows/kanvas.yml` | GitHub rejected the write because of the existing file. Delete or edit the file in the repository, then run the stage again. |
| `unable to install workflow in <repository>` | The request failed or timed out after 30 seconds. Run the stage again. |
| `repository must be in "owner/name" form` | The repository identifier is malformed. |

### If you uninstall the App

Cloud checks whether the App installation still exists. When GitHub reports that it does not, Cloud deletes the stale GitHub connection. Run the wizard again to reconnect.

## Use the action in your own workflow

Skip the wizard when you want to choose the triggers, run snapshots from a workflow you already maintain, or authenticate with a personal access token instead of the App.

1. Generate a Layer5 Cloud API token and store it as a repository secret, for example `MESHERY_TOKEN`.
2. Add a workflow. The action needs its own repository checked out to a folder named `action`, and the same token permissions the installed workflow uses.

```yaml
name: Kanvas Snapshot
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

permissions:
  actions: read
  contents: write
  security-events: write
  statuses: write
  pull-requests: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  snapshot:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          path: action
          repository: layer5labs/kanvas-snapshot
      - uses: layer5labs/kanvas-snapshot@v0.2.44
        with:
          githubToken: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          mesheryToken: ${{ secrets.MESHERY_TOKEN }}
          prNumber: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
          application_type: "Kubernetes Manifest"
          filePath: manifests
```

To snapshot a file that is hosted at a public URL, such as a packaged Helm chart, replace `filePath` with `application_url` and set `application_type` to `Helm Chart`. Pin the action to the latest release tag; `v0.2.44` is current at the time of writing.

### Action inputs

| Input | Required | Default | Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| `githubToken` | Yes | - | Posts the pull request comment. The built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` or a personal access token that can write pull request comments. |
| `mesheryToken` | Yes | - | Layer5 Cloud API token. |
| `application_type` | Yes | - | `Kubernetes Manifest`, `Docker Compose`, or `Helm Chart`. |
| `filePath` | No | - | A file, or a directory of manifests, in the checked-out repository. |
| `application_url` | No | - | A public URL of the source file. |
| `designID` | No | - | The id of an existing design. Overrides `filePath` and `application_url`. |
| `prNumber` | No | `0` | The pull request to comment on. With `0`, no comment is posted. |
| `skipComment` | No | `false` | Set to `true` to render without commenting, for manual or scheduled runs. |
| `assetLocation` | No | - | Where the rendered image is stored. |
| `email` | No | - | See [known limitations](#known-limitations). |

When you give `filePath` a directory, the action merges the `.yaml` and `.yml` files directly inside it into one document. It does not read subfolders. Point it at the folder that holds the manifests, or at a single file.

The action outputs `resource_url`, the URL of the rendered image. When no image URL comes back, the action does not post a comment.

### Choose other triggers

The comment needs a pull request number, so only pull request runs post one. Use any other workflow event, such as `push`, `schedule`, or `workflow_dispatch`, to render a snapshot without a comment and read `resource_url` in a later step. Leave `prNumber` at `0` or set `skipComment` to `true` for those runs.

## What the pull request comment contains

The comment shows the rendered image, linked to itself, with links to the generated design in the catalog and to an editable copy in the Playground. The workflow keeps one comment per pull request and replaces its content on each run.

Alongside the comment, each run uploads debug logs, screenshots, and a video of the render as workflow artifacts, whether the run succeeds or fails. Open them from the workflow run when a snapshot looks wrong.

## Change or remove snapshots

| To | Do this |
|---|---|
| Snapshot a different file | Run the wizard again and select another file, or edit `filePath` in the workflow. |
| Add a repository | Install the App on it, then run the wizard again. |
| Upgrade the action | Change the version tag after `layer5labs/kanvas-snapshot@` in the workflow. Check the release notes when `application_type` or input names change. |
| Rotate the token | Generate a new API token, update the `MESHERY_TOKEN` secret, and revoke the old token. |
| Remove snapshots | Delete `.github/workflows/kanvas.yml`, delete the `MESHERY_TOKEN` secret, and revoke the token. |

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| The workflow runs and no comment appears | The run had no pull request number, `skipComment` is `true`, or the render produced no image URL. Open the uploaded workflow artifacts to see why the render failed. |
| The snapshot shows nothing, or only some resources | A directory path reads only the YAML files directly inside it. Point `filePath` at the folder that holds them. |
| The snapshot treats a Helm chart or Compose file as a manifest | The wizard sets `application_type` to `Kubernetes Manifest`. Edit it in the workflow. |
| Authentication fails | `MESHERY_TOKEN` is missing, misspelled, or revoked, or the repository does not share the secret with the workflow. |
| The wizard lists no repositories | The App is not installed on them. Install it, then run the wizard again. |

## Known limitations

- **Email delivery.** The `email` input does not deliver mail today. The action sends its request in a shape the Layer5 Cloud endpoint rejects, and the workflow continues without a failure. Use the pull request comment or `resource_url`.
- **No diffs.** A snapshot shows the current file only. It does not compare against the base branch.
- **Single design per repository in the wizard.** To snapshot more than one file, add the action to a workflow of your own for each file.
- **GitHub.com only.** The App and the install flow work against github.com.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Create Relationships"
url: /kanvas/guides/designing/creating-relationships/index.md
description: Connect components with edges, nest them in parents, and remove or hide relationships. Covers which relationships you draw and which Kanvas forms for you.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Relationships record how components connect, and Kanvas keeps related configuration in sync once they exist. You create some relationships by hand and Kanvas creates others when it evaluates the design. This guide shows which is which, how to create each kind, and how to remove or hide them.

Relationships work only in Designer mode. For what each kind means, read [Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md" >}}).

| Kind | You create it by | You remove it by |
|---|---|---|
| Edge (network, mount, reference, and other edge subtypes) | Picking an edge from a component's handle and dragging to a target | Selecting the edge and choosing Delete |
| Hierarchical, inventory | Dropping a component onto a compatible parent | Dragging it out, or choosing Move Out of Parent |
| Hierarchical, wallet | Dropping a component onto a compatible host | Deleting the component, or choosing Move Out of Parent |
| Hierarchical, alias | Kanvas creates it during evaluation | Deleting the alias component |
| TagSets (shared labels) | Giving components matching labels | Changing the labels so they stop matching |
| Annotation edge | Drawing with the Pen tool | Selecting the edge and choosing Delete |

## Create an edge relationship

Edge relationships connect components that exchange traffic or depend on one another, such as a Service and a Deployment.

1. Hover a component to reveal arrow handles on its bottom, left, and right sides, then select one. A circular menu opens.
2. Pick a relationship from the menu. It lists every edge relationship in the registry that can start from this component, with the subtype in a tooltip. A binding relationship lists one item per component that can sit between the two ends.
3. Drag from the source to a target. Compatible targets in view get a green outline, and incompatible components dim to half opacity. Kanvas checks only the components visible in the viewport.
4. Release on a compatible target.

Releasing on an incompatible component, a non-component, or empty canvas cancels the creation without a message. A binding relationship also places its binding component between the two ends.

![Creating a network edge between two components](images/relationships/EdgeNetwork.gif)

The edge shows an arrow and a label. Network edges label the source and target ports and protocols, read from the configuration the relationship manages.

## Nest components in a parent

Drag a component onto another and release. Valid targets are the components that form an inventory or wallet relationship with it, and Kanvas outlines them in green while you drag. The same drop works when you drag a component from the palette onto an existing component.

- **Inventory.** The child is drawn inside the parent. For example, a Pod dropped on a Namespace becomes its child. You can collapse and expand parents.
- **Wallet.** The child is absorbed into the host and shown as a green badge at the host's bottom-right corner with the item count. Select the badge to list the items, then select an item to open its configurator. A sidecar attached to a workload is an example.

A component has at most one parent. Dropping it into a new parent replaces the old relationship, and dropping it on empty canvas removes it.

![Dropping a child component into a parent](images/relationships/create-parent-child.gif)

![A wallet badge showing attached items on the host component](images/relationships/create-inventory-wallet.gif)

## Let labels form TagSets

You never draw a TagSet. When components carry labels or annotations that match under a registry relationship definition, the next evaluation creates a TagSet and draws a translucent region around the group. See [Work with Tags]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/tagsets/index.md" >}}).

![Components with matching labels grouped into a TagSet](images/relationships/create-matchlabels.gif)

## Remove a relationship

- **Edge.** Select the edge and choose Delete in its toolbar. Kanvas marks the relationship deleted, and the next evaluation reverses its effects on configuration.
- **Inventory.** Drag the child out of the parent, or right-click it and choose Move Out of Parent.
- **Wallet.** No control deletes a wallet relationship by itself. Delete the component, or choose Move Out of Parent.
- **TagSet.** No control deletes a TagSet. Change the labels so they no longer match, or hide the layer.

![Deleting an edge relationship](images/relationships/delete-edge.gif)

![Dragging a child out of a parent](images/relationships/delete-parent-child.gif)

## Style an edge

Select an edge to open its toolbar. It offers line color, line style (solid, dashed, or dotted), curve and arrow style, a label, and an animation (none or marching ants). Styling changes only appearance.

## Hide a kind of relationship

The Layers panel lists eight relationship kinds, each with a count and a show or hide toggle: hierarchical inventory, wallet, and alias; TagSets; and edge mount, network, annotation, and reference. Open the panel with the backslash key or from the design toolbar.

Hiding a kind removes it from the canvas. It does not stop evaluation. Kanvas still evaluates the whole design, so configuration that a hidden relationship manages keeps syncing. The toggles are stored in the design, so they are saved with it, restored when it reopens, and shared with collaborators. Everything is visible by default.

![The Layers panel with relationship toggles](images/relationships/layers-panel-relationships.gif)

## Configuration sync

When two components are related, the registry definition names which fields on each side are linked, and Kanvas writes values across them each time it evaluates the design. For example, changing a Service's port updates the matching container port on a related Deployment. The relationship definition decides the direction, so it can differ by kind. See [Policy Evaluation]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationship-evaluation/index.md" >}}).

## Limits

- Kanvas draws at most 30 TagSets. Beyond that, it shows the warning "Skipped rendering of N matchlabels relationships due to limit of 30".
- TagSets render only in Full render fidelity.
- No other kind has a rendering limit.

## See also

- [Add and Configure Components]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/configuring-components/index.md" >}}): the Relationships tab lists each component's relationships.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Share a Design Across Organizations"
url: /kanvas/tutorials/stellar-saas-platform/index.md
description: Grant a reviewer in another organization access to a private design, run the review in comments, and revoke access when the review ends.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this tutorial, an Organization Admin at one company asks an engineer at another company to review a private design. By the end, you will have given someone outside your organization access to one design, held a review in a comment thread, and removed that access. Along the way, you will learn what a grant gives someone, where Kanvas checks permissions, and why the review itself has to happen in comments.

The cast is the same one used across these docs (see [Meet Five and the Cast]({{< ref "cloud/getting-started/meet-five/_index.md" >}})). Marcus Webb is the Organization Admin at Stellar Dynamics. Five is a Platform Engineer at Orbital Labs, a separate organization.

## Before you begin

- Marcus holds the **Share Design permission** in Stellar Dynamics. Kanvas checks it in the organization that owns the design's workspace, so a grant from another organization does not count.
- Marcus holds the **View All Users** permission. The people picker in the Share dialog depends on it.
- Five holds **View All Users** as well, so he can @mention Marcus in a comment.
- Both accounts exist on the same Layer5 Cloud.
- The design is saved and private. A design gets a link only after its first save gives it an id. Kanvas hides Share for empty designs and for published designs.

## The scenario

Marcus owns a saved design called `stellar-saas-platform`. It models Stellar Dynamics' Azure SaaS stack: an AKS cluster, Azure SQL, API Management, Azure AD, Event Hub, and the connections between them. Before his team runs it in production, he wants Five to review the architecture.

## Step 1: Marcus grants Five access

Marcus opens the Share dialog on `stellar-saas-platform` and searches for Five by name. The search covers every user Marcus's role lets him search, not just members of Stellar Dynamics, so Five appears even though he belongs to Orbital Labs. Marcus adds Five, and Five now appears in the list of people with access.

Here is the model to remember. **A private design opens for its owner, for provider administrators, and for each person who holds a grant on it.** A grant links one person to one design. It has no access level and never checks organizations. Kanvas does not compare Five's organization with the design's, and you do not need any provider-level trust setting.

An invitation email goes out only when the share request asks for one, so Marcus copies the design link and sends it to Five himself.

**Result:** Five holds a grant on `stellar-saas-platform`.

## Step 2: Five opens the design

Five follows the link while signed in to his Orbital Labs account. The design loads with every component and connection Marcus drew. It also appears in Five's list of designs shared with him.

Five gets this one design and nothing else. The grant does not make him a member of Stellar Dynamics. Other private designs in the same workspace remain closed to him, because each private design checks its own grants. Assigning a team to the workspace would not open them either.

**Result:** Five sees the design Marcus sees.

## Step 3: Five comments and mentions Marcus

Five places a comment next to API Management and writes:

> @Marcus Webb You're missing a WAF in front of API Management.

Typing `@` followed by part of a name brings up matching users. Choosing one stores a real mention, not plain text.

The comment is a component in the design, so it saves and travels with the design. If Marcus has the design open, the comment shows up on his canvas right away. Because Five mentioned him, Marcus also gets an email with the design's name, a snapshot, and the thread, unless he has turned off comment emails in his account preferences.

**Result:** An open thread on the design names Marcus.

## Step 4: Marcus responds, edits, and resolves

Marcus replies in the thread. Five wrote an earlier message in it, so Five receives an email about the reply. Marcus then adds an Azure Application Gateway in front of API Management and connects the two. Kanvas autosaves the change.

Marcus resolves the thread. The comment leaves the canvas but stays in the comments panel under the Resolved filter. Resolving sends no email. If anyone posts again in the thread, it reopens.

**Result:** The fix is in the design, and the thread records why it was made.

## What this means for review

Kanvas has no view-only or comment-only grant. A grantee can do anything an editor can do. Five can open the design, save edits, comment, clone it, download it, and switch it between private and public. He can only re-share it if his role gives him the Share Design permission in Stellar Dynamics' organization. Five cannot delete the design, and he cannot take over ownership.

The rules of the review therefore live in the comment thread, not in the permission system. Marcus has two tools for keeping it that way:

- **Remove the grant when the review ends.** Access lasts exactly as long as the grant does.
- **Offer a clone.** If Five wants to experiment, a clone gives him an independent copy, and the original stays untouched.

For live co-editing during a review, see [Collaborative Editing]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/collaborative-editing.md" >}}).

## Step 5: Marcus revokes access

Once the review is done, Marcus removes Five from the list of people with access in the Share dialog. When Five opens the link again, Kanvas refuses it, and the design leaves his shared list.

Five's comments stay in the design. Comments are part of the design, so removing a person does not remove what they wrote. A clone is a separate design, so revoking access to the original does not affect any clone Five made.

**Result:** Only Marcus and provider administrators can open `stellar-saas-platform`.

## Access at a glance

This table applies to a private design. Provider administrators can open and delete any private design.

| Person | Open the private design | Edit it | Comment | Re-share | Delete |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Marcus (owner) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, with the Share Design permission | Yes |
| Five (grantee) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Only with the Share Design permission in the design's organization | No |
| Someone with no grant | No | No | No | No | No |

## Next steps

- [Share a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md" >}}) covers granting, revoking, and changing visibility.
- [Review a Design with Comments]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/reviewing-designs/index.md" >}}) covers comment threads, mentions, filters, and notifications.
- [Collaboration Model]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/collaboration/index.md" >}}) explains how sharing, comments, and live editing fit together.
- [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}) lists every permission that controls these actions.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Deploy and Observe Your First Design"
url: /kanvas/getting-started/design-to-deployment/index.md
description: Validate and dry-run your first design, deploy it to a Kubernetes cluster, find its running resources in Operator mode, and undeploy it.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this tutorial you take the design you saved in [Create Your First Design]({{< ref "kanvas/getting-started/starting-scratch.md" >}}) to a live Kubernetes cluster. You validate it, dry-run it against the cluster, deploy it, and then switch to Operator mode to see the running resources that belong to the design. You finish by undeploying it.

Along the way you learn the difference between checking a design against its schemas and checking it against a cluster, how Kanvas chooses where to deploy, and how Kanvas keeps track of the resources a design creates.

{{< alert type="info" title="This tutorial needs a Meshery you run" >}}
Hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new cannot validate, dry-run, deploy, or undeploy designs, and it does not offer Operator mode. On kanvas.new these actions open a prompt that sends you to a Meshery you run instead. Use the [Meshery Playground](https://playground.meshery.io) or [install Meshery](https://docs.meshery.io/installation/) in your own environment, then open your design there.
{{< /alert >}}

## Before you begin

You need:

- **The `web-app` design** from the previous tutorial, saved and open in Designer mode.
- **A Meshery you run**, either the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery, signed in with Layer5 Cloud as its provider. Operator views are stored in Layer5 Cloud, so the local provider cannot show them.
- **A connected Kubernetes cluster** with Meshery Operator deployed. Meshery Operator installs MeshSync and Meshery Broker in the cluster; MeshSync streams the cluster's live state to Meshery Server, and that stream is what Operator mode displays. See [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}).
- **Permissions** in your organization for each action. Validate Design permits both validation and dry runs, Deploy Design permits deploying, and Undeploy Design permits undeploying. When you lack one of these permissions, the matching action is not available to you.

## Step 1: Validate the design

Validate the design from the design's action toolbar. Kanvas shows "Validating design" and opens a dialog titled `Validate design "web-app"`.

**What Kanvas does:** validation checks every component in the design against that component's schema. It does not contact any cluster. Each error is attached to the component and the field that caused it, so you fix problems where they are, not in a separate list. When validation of the whole design completes, Kanvas records a validation event in your Layer5 Cloud event log.

**What you should see:** no errors for this design. If validation finds problems, Kanvas shows "Design validation error" and marks the affected components. Open each marked component, correct the field, and validate again.

## Step 2: Dry-run the design against the cluster

Start a dry run. Kanvas opens a dialog titled `Dryrun design "web-app"`.

**What Kanvas does:** a dry run sends the design to the target cluster for checking without applying anything. It catches problems that schemas cannot, the ones only the cluster knows about. Dry-run errors attach to components in the same way as schema errors, so both kinds appear side by side on the affected component.

Validation answers "is this design well formed?". A dry run answers "would this cluster accept it?". Run both before every deployment.

**What you should see:** a dry run that completes without errors. Nothing has changed in the cluster yet.

## Step 3: Deploy the design

Deploy the design. Kanvas opens a dialog titled `Deploy design "web-app"` that walks you through the deployment.

**What Kanvas does:** Kanvas applies the design to the Kubernetes contexts you select. If you do not select any, Kanvas deploys to **all** connected clusters. Choose your target deliberately when more than one cluster is connected.

Every resource Kanvas creates carries the design's identity:

| Metadata | Key | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Label | `design.meshery.io/id` | The design's ID |
| Annotation | `design.meshery.io/version` | The design version that was deployed |
| Annotation | `component.meshery.io/id` | The ID of the component the resource came from |

The label is what makes a resource "managed by Meshery". It also lets you find the design's resources with your own tools, for example `kubectl get all -l design.meshery.io/id=<design-id>`.

**What you should see:** the deployment completes, and the Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap exist in the cluster.

## Step 4: Observe the design in Operator mode

Switch from Designer to Operator mode.

If the design has unsaved changes, Kanvas asks "You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?" before it switches. Confirm only if you are ready to lose those changes; otherwise stay, let the design save, and switch again.

**What Kanvas does:** Operator mode shows the recorded state of your clusters through views. A view is a saved set of filters. A new, empty view shows Nodes and Namespaces across the clusters you select. A design's view is named after the design, `web-app-View`, and filters on the design's `design.meshery.io/id` label, so it shows only the resources this design created.

**What you should see:** in the design's view, the running Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap from your design, and nothing else from the cluster.

## Step 5: Undeploy the design

Return to Designer mode and undeploy the design. Kanvas opens a dialog titled `Undeploy design "web-app"`.

**What Kanvas does:** undeploy removes the design's resources from the Kubernetes contexts you select. As with deploy, selecting no context targets **all** connected clusters. You can dry-run an undeploy first to see what it would do.

**What you should see:** the undeploy completes and the resources are removed from the cluster. The design itself stays saved, ready to deploy again.

## If something goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A prompt says Operator mode is not available on kanvas.new. | Hosted Kanvas cannot validate, deploy, undeploy, connect clusters, or open Operator mode. | Open the design in the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery. |
| Validate, dry run, deploy, and undeploy are disabled. | The design is empty. These actions need at least one component. | Add components to the design, or open the saved `web-app` design. |
| One of the actions is not available to you. | Your role in the organization lacks the matching permission: Validate Design, Deploy Design, or Undeploy Design. | Ask an organization administrator to grant the permission. |
| "Design validation error" appears. | One or more components fail their schema. | Open each marked component, correct the field the error is attached to, and validate again. |
| A dry run reports errors on components. | The target cluster would reject part of the design. | Correct the marked components, then run the dry run again before you deploy. |
| Kanvas asks "You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?" | The design has changes that are not saved yet. | Cancel, let autosave finish or save the design, then switch modes. |
| Resources appeared in clusters you did not intend. | No Kubernetes context was selected, so the action targeted all connected clusters. | Undeploy from the unintended clusters, then select contexts explicitly before you deploy again. |

## What you learned

- Validation checks a design against component schemas; a dry run checks it against a cluster. Neither changes the cluster.
- Deploy and undeploy act on the contexts you select, and on every connected cluster when you select none.
- Every deployed resource is labeled with the design's ID, which is how Operator mode filters the cluster inventory down to one design.
- Switching modes with unsaved changes asks for confirmation.
- Each action is gated by its own permission.

## Next

- [Validating designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/validating-designs/index.md" >}})
- [Dry-running a design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/dry-running-a-design/index.md" >}})
- [Deploying designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}})
- [Undeploying designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/undeploying-designs/index.md" >}})
- [Operator]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/operator/index.md" >}}), to explore views and live cluster state beyond a single design.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Dry-run a Design"
url: /kanvas/guides/deploying/dry-running-a-design/index.md
description: Preview what a deployment would do by having each target cluster's Kubernetes API check your design without applying it.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A dry run submits every component in the design to the Kubernetes API server of each target cluster as a server-side dry-run request. The API server validates the object exactly as it would on a real apply, including schema, field values, and admission, and then discards it. Nothing is created, updated, or persisted, so you can repeat a dry run as often as you like.

## Before you start

- **A connected cluster.** Meshery must hold at least one connected Kubernetes context. With none, the request fails with error `meshery-server-1096`, Kubernetes cluster is unavailable.
- **A non-empty design.** The Actions menu is disabled for an empty design.
- **Permission.** Dry run is gated by the Validate Design permission. See [Permissions by Role]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/permissions.md" >}}).
- **A Meshery you run.** The hosted kanvas.new site does not run dry runs.

Meshery Server performs the dry run with the kubeconfig it holds. Meshery Operator, MeshSync, and the broker are not required.

## Run a dry run

You reach a dry run in two ways.

**On its own.** Choose Dry Run from the design's Actions menu. This opens `Dryrun design "<name>"` and runs a deploy-type dry run against your current cluster selection, or against all connected clusters when none is selected. There is no cluster-selection step.

**Inside a deploy or undeploy.** Step 3 of both steppers is a dry run against the environments you chose in step 2. In the deploy stepper it simulates creating the resources. In the undeploy stepper it simulates deleting them. See [Deploy a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/deploying-designs/index.md" >}}) and [Undeploy a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/undeploying-designs/index.md" >}}).

On mobile, Dry Run runs without a modal and shows its results as badges on the canvas.

## What the server does

| Stage | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Components | Annotation components are dropped. Each remaining component becomes a Kubernetes object. |
| Clusters | The object goes to every selected cluster. |
| Deploy-type | A create with strict field validation and field manager `meshery`. |
| Undeploy-type | A delete by name. |
| Namespace | The component's own `metadata.namespace`. Otherwise `default` for namespaced kinds, and none for cluster-scoped kinds. |
| Persistence | None. The dry run does not create namespaces. |

## Read the results

The summary shows `<N> component(s) and <M> annotations` and the error count. With no errors it reads `No deployment errors.`

Each failing component is an expandable row, `<name> (<count>)`. A component fails when any selected cluster returns a Kubernetes failure for it. Each error shows a bold type and field path, then the message the API server returned:

- The type is the Kubernetes cause in words: Field Value Required, Field Value Invalid, Field Value Not Supported. Anything else shows as Failure.
- The path reads `<component> > settings > <field>`. Metadata name, namespace, labels, and annotations map to those names. When Kubernetes names no field the path is `unknown`.
- When the API gives no causes, its status messages appear as plain text.

If the whole call fails rather than a component, a structured error block appears with the entry type `RequestError`, not a per-component row.

Selecting an error closes the results and opens the component's configuration at the field. Errors also feed the red octagon badge on the canvas. See [Validate a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/deploying/validating-designs/index.md" >}}) for where badges appear.

Each dry run records an event: `Dry Run completed for design '<name>'.` at informational severity, even when components failed, or `Failed to dry-run design '<name>'.` at error severity when the call itself failed. A dry run does not change the design's deployment count.

## Common errors

| Error | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Field Value Invalid | A value is outside what Kubernetes accepts, for example a Service port of 0 where 1 to 65535 is required. | Correct the value in the component's configuration. |
| Field Value Required | A required field is empty. | Fill in the field. |
| Resource not found for a component of a kind with an irregular plural | See the limits below. | Bypass the error if the kind is correct. |
| Missing custom resource definition | The design uses a custom resource whose definition is not on the cluster. | Install the definition on the cluster first, then run the dry run again. |

## Limits of a dry run

- **Irregular plurals.** Dry run builds each resource name from the lowercase kind plus "s". Kinds with irregular plurals, such as Ingress, NetworkPolicy, StorageClass, and Endpoints, can return a not-found error even when the component is correct.
- **Namespaces the design creates.** A dry run never creates a namespace. A component placed in a namespace that the same design would create reports an error, because the namespace does not exist yet.
- **Undeploy-type runs.** Deleting an object that is absent returns NotFound. Dry-running the undeploy of a design that was never deployed, or is already removed, shows an error for every component. A real undeploy ignores objects that are already absent.
- **The Include Dependencies option.** The dry-run step shows an Include Dependencies checkbox. It has no effect on the dry run.

## Bypass errors

In the deploy and undeploy steppers, when a dry run reports errors, the step shows a checkbox, `Bypass errors and initiate deployment`. Next stays disabled while the dry run is running, or while errors exist and the checkbox is off. Use the bypass when you know the errors are false positives from the limits above. The cluster raised each of them, and the real deployment may fail for the same reason.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Permissions by Role"
url: /kanvas/reference/permissions/index.md
description: Which Kanvas actions are checked against a permission, which default role grants each permission, what anonymous users can do, and which actions are limited by mode and ownership instead.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This page tells you which Kanvas actions require a permission, which default roles grant each permission, and which actions are limited by something other than a permission. Use it to find out why an action is missing for a user and which role grants it.

## How permissions work

A permission is a named key, such as Deploy Design, that allows one action. Keys are grouped into keychains, and a role bundles one or more keychains. Your organization assigns roles to users. Before Kanvas offers certain actions, it checks whether the user holds the matching key. Kanvas uses the shared Layer5 permission set and defines no permissions of its own. See [Roles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/_index.md" >}}) and [Keychains]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/keychains.md" >}}).

## Where Kanvas checks a permission

Kanvas checks a permission before it offers each of the following actions:

| Action | Permission checked | Also note |
|---|---|---|
| Validate and Dry run | Validate Design | One permission controls both actions. Disabled while the design is empty. |
| Deploy | Deploy Design | Disabled while the design is empty. |
| Undeploy | Undeploy Design | Disabled while the design is empty. |
| Share | Share Design | Also hidden while the design is empty or published. |
| Publish | Publish Design | Anonymous users get a sign-in prompt instead. |
| Operator mode | None | The provider enables Operator mode. When the provider does not enable it, the Operator switch is disabled. |

When a user does not hold the permission, Kanvas does not offer the action: the toolbar hides it or shows it disabled, and the action sheet on small screens omits it.

Layer5 Cloud also enforces permissions when it receives a request, independently of the Kanvas interface. It checks Share Design when a design is shared, View Designs when a user reads other members' private designs, the workspace permissions when designs or views are assigned to or removed from a workspace, and Share Views when a view is shared.

## Default role access

The tables below show which default roles grant each design and view permission. They are refreshed automatically from the Layer5 permission list.

- A check mark means the role grants the permission.
- A check mark with an asterisk means the role grants the permission only on resources the user owns.
- A dash means the role does not grant the permission.

{{< keys-matrix caption="Design lifecycle" functions="Validate Design|Deploy Design|Undeploy Design|Share Design|Publish Design|Unpublish Design|Clone Design|View Designs|Assign Designs to Workspaces|Remove Designs from Workspaces" >}}

{{< keys-matrix caption="Views and clusters" functions="View Views|Assign Views to Workspace|Unassign Views from Workspace|Add cluster|View All Kubernetes Clusters" >}}

Org Admin is the Organization Admin role. The roles not shown, Org Billing Manager and the Academy roles, hold none of these permissions. Provider Admin holds every permission.

## Anonymous users

A user is anonymous when no one is signed in or the signed-in account has anonymous status. An anonymous user authors and edits designs. Sharing or publishing a design opens a sign-in prompt that names the feature and offers a single Sign in action.

Anonymous users receive the anonymous role. It holds the same canvas permissions as the User role, plus Screenshot Canvas and View help center. It does not hold the Operator terminal, metrics, or component details permissions.

On [kanvas.new](https://kanvas.new), Validate, Dry run, Deploy, Undeploy, connecting a cluster, and Operator mode open a prompt that directs the user to the [Meshery Playground](https://playground.meshery.io) or a self-hosted Meshery deployment. This applies to signed-in users on kanvas.new as well. See [Feature Availability by Plan]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/feature-availability.md" >}}).

## What is not gated per action

### Canvas editing

Kanvas does not check a permission for individual canvas edits: adding, deleting, cloning, copying, locking, and styling components, shapes, text boxes, sections, and comments; undo and redo; and the pen and pencil tools. Roles carry permissions with these names, but removing them from a role does not prevent the edit. Three things limit canvas editing instead:

- **Mode.** Designer mode allows authoring. Operator mode does not.
- **Node kind.** Live nodes, the resources Kanvas reads from a connected cluster, are read-only in every mode.
- **Design ownership and sharing.** A user edits a design they own or one that is shared with them.

### Operator mode

Operator mode blocks canvas authoring: dropping, editing, duplicating, deleting, and renaming nodes are not allowed. Operator mode is not read-only, though. From Operator, a user still opens terminal and exec sessions and generates load.

### Terminal, log streaming, and performance tests

The Kanvas interface does not check a permission before it opens a terminal session, streams container logs, or runs a performance test. Layer5 Cloud defines the permissions Stream container logs, Perform performance test in Operator, and Select performance profile in Operator. By default, only Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold them.

## Customizing access

Enterprise plans can define custom roles built from keychains, so you can grant a group exactly the permissions it needs, such as Validate Design without Deploy Design. In the Kanvas interface, a custom role changes what is offered only for the actions listed in [Where Kanvas checks a permission](#where-kanvas-checks-a-permission); Layer5 Cloud applies its own checks to sharing, private designs, and workspace assignments. See [Roles]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/roles/_index.md" >}}).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Relationships"
url: /kanvas/concepts/relationships/index.md
description: What relationships are, the kinds Kanvas draws and evaluates, how each one forms, and how relationships keep component configuration consistent.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A relationship records how two components connect: one runs inside the other, one sends traffic to the other, one mounts the other's storage, or both carry the same label. Relationships do more than draw lines. Each relationship definition names the configuration fields on both sides that must agree, so Kanvas can write values from one component into the other and keep the design consistent as you edit. The definitions come from the Meshery registry, not from Kanvas, so the set of relationships available to you depends on the models you use.

## Kinds of relationship

The Layers panel lists eight kinds of relationship, which fall into three families.

### Edge relationships

An edge is a line between two components that interact. You draw it by hand. Kanvas lists the edges the registry allows from the component you start on, and highlights the targets that are compatible.

| Subtype | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Network | Traffic can flow between the components. The edge labels source and target ports and protocols. | A Service gives a stable endpoint to a Deployment's replicas. |
| Mount | One component gives storage or files to another, through a binding component placed between them. | A PersistentVolume mounted into a Pod. |
| Reference | One component points to another by name, identifier, or scope. It declares a dependency and does not itself grant access or carry traffic. | A Pod that references a ConfigMap or a Secret. |
| Annotation | A line you draw with the Pen tool to explain flow. It has no effect on configuration. | A traced request path on a diagram. |

![An edge network relationship between a Service and a Deployment](images/EdgeNetworkRelationship.svg)

![An edge mount relationship between a PersistentVolume and a Pod](images/EdgeMountRelationship.svg)

![An edge reference relationship from a Deployment to a ConfigMap](images/reference-deployment-configmap.png)

The registry can define other edge subtypes. They appear in the edge picker when they can start from the selected component.

### Hierarchical relationships

A hierarchical relationship nests one component in another. A component has at most one parent.

- **Inventory.** The child is drawn inside its parent, as a Pod sits inside a Namespace. Because the Namespace's name is the Pod's namespace, the parent's configuration flows to the child.
- **Wallet.** The child is absorbed into its host and shown as a count badge on the host, as a sidecar is attached to a workload.
- **Alias.** The child stands for one field inside its parent. Editing the alias edits that field of the parent.

![A hierarchical parent relationship between a Namespace and a Pod](images/Hierarchical_Parent_Relationship.svg)

### TagSets

Components that carry matching labels or annotations form a TagSet. Kanvas never asks you to draw one. It appears when the labels match and disappears when they stop matching. See [Work with Tags]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/tagsets/index.md" >}}).

![A TagSet drawn around components with matching labels](images/tags.png)

## How relationships form

Three mechanisms create relationships:

| Mechanism | Kinds |
|---|---|
| You create them: drag an edge, drop a component into a parent, or draw with the Pen | Edge, inventory, wallet, annotation |
| Evaluation creates them from the registry definitions | TagSets, alias, and any relationship the definitions say should exist |
| Paste or duplicate copies them with the components | Any relationship whose two ends are both in the copied set |

Deleting a component marks the relationships that touched it as deleted. The next evaluation then reverses their effects on configuration.

## Relationships keep configuration in sync

Evaluation is the process that applies relationship definitions to a design. It runs shortly after a change, writes values across related fields, and can add or remove components and relationships. The direction of a write depends on the definition and the kind.

| Kind | Typical direction | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Inventory | Parent to child | The child takes its namespace from the parent Namespace. |
| Edge | Source to target | A Service's port is written into the related Deployment's container port. |
| Wallet | Attached item to host | The host takes the item's configuration. |

Treat these as typical. The relationship definition is the authority, and Kanvas does not hard-code a direction. [Policy Evaluation]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/relationship-evaluation/index.md" >}}) explains when evaluation runs and why results can change after you stop editing.

## What relationships mean at deploy time

Annotation edges, TagSets, and the drawing of any relationship never change what Kanvas deploys by themselves. What gets deployed is the configuration of each component. Relationships matter because they decided what that configuration is.

## Related pages

- [Create Relationships]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designing/creating-relationships/index.md" >}}): create, remove, and hide relationships.
- [Designs and Components]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/designs/index.md" >}}): what a design contains.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Review a Design with Comments"
url: /kanvas/guides/collaborating/reviewing-designs/index.md
description: Leave threaded comments on a design, mention collaborators, resolve and reopen threads, and control who gets emailed.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A comment is a note on the canvas that holds a threaded conversation. Use comments to give feedback, record the reason behind a configuration choice, or ask a teammate a question next to the component it concerns. A comment is part of the design: it saves with the design, appears live to everyone who has the design open, and travels with clones and exports.

For how comments fit with live editing and access, read [Collaboration Model]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/collaboration/index.md" >}}).

## Who can comment

Anyone who can open a design can comment on it. The role catalog lists separate permissions for adding, resolving, deleting, and styling comments, but Kanvas does not enforce them. Whoever can edit a design can do every comment action. Comments work in Designer mode only.

Because new designs are public, a comment on a public design is visible to anyone who opens it. To limit who sees your review, make the design private and share it with the reviewers. See [Share a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md" >}}).

<figure>
  <img src="images/kanvas-comment.png" alt="A comment thread on the Designer canvas showing several messages from different people" />
  <figcaption>A comment thread on the canvas.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Add a comment

Add a comment in any of three ways:

- Drag the Comment tool from the dock onto the canvas, or click it to drop a comment near the center.
- Right-click the canvas and choose Add Comment. The comment lands where you clicked.
- Press <kbd>M</kbd>. The comment appears near the center of the canvas, and you can drag it into place.

A comment is an annotation component, so it moves, locks, groups, copies, and deletes like other annotations. See [Canvas Objects]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-objects/index.md" >}}). The Annotations toggle in the Layers panel hides all annotations, comments included, on your canvas. Hidden comments still sync.

## Hold a conversation

Each comment holds one thread. Type a message and press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to send it. Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> or <kbd>Cmd</kbd> with <kbd>Enter</kbd> to add a line break. A message cannot be empty. A thread shows its first message and offers to show the rest when it has more than one.

A message can contain:

- **Mentions.** Type `@` and the start of a name. The picker searches every user on the platform, not only people with access to the design, and shows up to seven matches. A bare `@` shows none. The search needs the View All Users permission. If it fails, Kanvas shows an error instead of "no users".
- **Links.** URLs become links.
- **Emoji.** Type `:` and part of an emoji name to pick one.

Messages cannot be edited, and a single message cannot be deleted. Deleting a comment removes the whole thread. Resolve a thread instead of deleting it when you want to keep the record.

### Resolve and reopen

Resolve a thread when the discussion is done. A resolved comment leaves the canvas but stays in the design with all its messages. Reopen it to bring it back. Adding a message to a resolved thread reopens it. Resolving and reopening send no notification.

### Find threads in the comments panel

The Comments panel lists every comment that has at least one message, newest activity first. Filter it by:

| Filter | Shows |
|---|---|
| All | Every comment with a message |
| Open | Threads that are not resolved |
| Resolved | Resolved threads |
| For me | Threads where any message mentions you |

The panel uses the same thread control as the canvas, so you can read, reply, resolve, reopen, and mute from it.

### Reuse a comment

Copy, paste, and duplicate create a new comment with the original's messages, timestamps, and name. The new comment is independent: editing or deleting the original does not change it. Copying or duplicating sends no notification. A reply to the copy notifies participants in the copy's thread. Pasting a comment into another design does not change who can open that design, so participants from the original thread may be unable to open the copy's design.

## Notifications {#managing-comment-notifications}

Kanvas sends comment notifications by email when a message is added. Resolving and reopening a thread send nothing.

Kanvas emails these people, after removing the author of the new message:

| Recipient | Receives email when |
|---|---|
| Mentioned users | The new message mentions them |
| Thread participants | They wrote an earlier message in the thread, or an earlier message mentioned them |
| The design owner | Someone other than the owner added the message |

A request is sent only when the message mentions someone, or the thread already has an earlier message by or mentioning another person. **A first comment that mentions nobody emails nobody, including the design owner.** Mention the owner when you need them to see a new comment.

An email goes out only if the recipient's account preferences allow it. Two preferences apply: comments on your designs, which governs the owner's email, and participating and mentions in comments, which governs the other two. See [Notification Preferences]({{< ref "cloud/concepts/identity-and-security/users/notification-preferences/index.md" >}}).

Kanvas does not check that a recipient can open the design before it emails them. The email shows the thread and links to the design in the Meshery Playground, whichever Meshery the design is stored for.

If a message posts but the emails fail, Kanvas shows "Comment posted, but the mentioned users could not be notified" and the reason. The comment stays.

Kanvas does not track which messages a person has read. Someone who misses an email learns of the comment only from a later notification or by opening the design.

### Mute a thread {#mute-comment-notifications}

Use the bell in a thread to stop mention and participant emails to you for that thread. The bell toggles your mute. The mute is stored in the thread, so it saves with the design and every collaborator can see the list of people who muted it.

Muting affects only the thread where you set it. Mentions in other threads and designs still reach you. The owner's email is decided by the commenter's mute list, not the owner's: a thread the owner muted still emails the owner, and a thread the commenter muted does not.

Account preferences apply to every design. A disabled preference stops those emails everywhere.

## Review practices that match how Kanvas works

- **Mention the person you need.** Mentions are the dependable notification path.
- **Resolve instead of delete.** Resolution keeps the discussion for later.
- **Review in a private, shared design.** Everyone with access can also edit, so agree who changes the design and who comments.
- **Use the For me filter after time away.** It lists threads that mention you.

## Related

- [Collaboration Model]({{< ref "kanvas/concepts/collaboration/index.md" >}})
- [Share a Design]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/collaborating/sharing-designs/index.md" >}})
- [Collaborative Editing]({{< ref "kanvas/tutorials/collaborative-editing.md" >}})
- [Canvas Objects]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/canvas-objects/index.md" >}})
- [Keyboard Shortcuts]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/keyboard-shortcuts.md" >}})


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Save Designs"
url: /kanvas/guides/designs/saving-designs/index.md
description: How Kanvas saves a design automatically, what the save indicator reports, how to save a copy, and what happens when a save fails.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Kanvas saves a design for you. There is no Save button and no Save shortcut. Every change that alters the design, such as adding, moving, configuring, or deleting a component, renaming, editing a relationship, or merging, queues a save. The request is sent 3 seconds after your last change. Changes made while a save is in flight queue a new save when it finishes.

Saving needs a signed-in user or a guest session on kanvas.new, and an organization. It does not check a permission key.

## What triggers a save, and what does not

A new design with no id is saved only once it has at least one component, or a name that is neither empty nor "Untitled Design". A design that was saved before is always saved.

Kanvas does not save when you load a design, when the server assigns the id after the first save, when you open a component configurator, or when collaborators' document updates arrive.

The first save creates the design, and the address bar updates to `?mode=design&design=<id>`. If you edit again before the first save returns, Kanvas holds the second save until the id arrives, so no duplicate design is created.

## Read the save indicator

The cloud icon in the top bar reports the state and doubles as a manual save trigger.

| State | Indicator |
|---|---|
| Saving | Animated icon and "Saving..." |
| Saved | "Saved" for 3 seconds, then a tooltip reading "All changes saved" with the time |
| Failed | Red cloud-off icon and "Unable to save. Retrying..." |

The tooltip on any saved design includes **View Save History**.

## Save a copy

**Save as** saves the open design as a new design with a name you enter. It proposes `<current name>-copy`. The copy gets a new id, you as owner, your selected workspace, public visibility, and version 0.0.1, then Kanvas loads it. The original is unchanged. Save as is disabled on an empty canvas. The name is required but not checked for length or uniqueness.

A new blank design is named "Untitled Design" until you rename it.

## Versions and history

Each save raises the patch number of the design's version: the first save is 0.0.1, the next 0.0.2, and so on. Autosaves, visibility changes, and catalog data edits all count, so the version tracks how often the design was saved, not meaningful releases. Cloning and imports reset the version to 0.0.1. There is no way to bump the major or minor number.

**View Save History** opens a list titled "Design Version History". It is an event log of who changed the design and when. You cannot restore, diff, or export an earlier version from it. If you need a version you can return to, export a copy at that point. See [Export Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/export-designs/index.md" >}}).

## Concurrent edits

Saving sends the whole design and the server overwrites the stored copy. The last save wins. Collaborators editing the same open design are reconciled live in the editor by the collaboration session, not at the storage layer.

## Plan limit: components per design

The server rejects a save when the design has more components than your plan allows.

| Plan | Components per design |
|---|---|
| Personal | 100 |
| Team Designer | 200 |
| Team Operator | 100 |
| Enterprise | 300 |

These are the seeded plan values. A deployment can differ. The limit applies to every save, to Save as, to merges, and to URL imports. It does not apply to cloning. A cloned design that exceeds your limit opens normally but fails its first save.

The server answers 403 with the message "Design exeeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan" (the misspelling ships) and an upgrade remediation. Kanvas does not show that message. You see only "Unable to save. Retrying..." and the edits stay on the canvas, unsaved. Reduce the component count below the limit to save again. An organization with no active subscription that grants the feature gets "Org is not entitled to adding components to a design".

For the other limits Layer5 lists per plan, see [Feature Availability]({{< ref "kanvas/reference/feature-availability.md" >}}). Plan limits other than components per design are not enforced when you save.

## When a save fails

| Message | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Failed to reach the cloud. Any changes made may not be saved. | The server was unreachable (HTTP 503). |
| Failed to save Design with name: <name> | Any other failure, including the plan limit. |
| Failed to save Design with name: <name> Design is invalid or empty | The design payload was empty or invalid. |

After a failure the editor enters an error mode: the top bar is tinted, and design-changing actions are ignored until the next command resets it. Autosave retries with exponential backoff, waiting 3 seconds times 2 to the power of the attempt number (6, 12, 24 seconds, and so on), up to 100 attempts. Any new edit resets the count.

Closing the tab or switching designs with unsaved changes asks "You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?"

## Who can save what

Anonymous users save normally into a guest account with its own organization and workspace. On sign-in, guest designs migrate to the account.

Updating an existing design keeps the original owner, visibility, and source type when the update does not state them. Operator mode blocks design edits, so it never saves a design. See [Manage Designs]({{< ref "kanvas/guides/designs/_index.md" >}}) for the defaults.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title: "Snapshot a Helm Chart"
